questions.stem: Hence, prove that \(\dfrac{22}{7}\) is an overestimate of \(\pi\) by evaluating the integral \(\int_0^1\dfrac{x^4(1-x)^4}{1+x^2}dx\).
questions.answer: Long division gives \(\dfrac{x^4(1-x)^4}{1+x^2}=x^6-4x^5+5x^4-4x^2+4-\dfrac{4}{1+x^2}\). Integrating from 0 to 1 gives \(\dfrac{22}{7}-\pi\), which is positive, so \(\dfrac{22}{7}>\pi\).

steps.explain: Long division of \(x^8-4x^7+6x^6-4x^5+x^4\) by \(1+x^2\) gives quotient \(x^6-4x^5+5x^4-4x^2+4\) and remainder \(-4\).

Integrate from 0 to 1 term by term: \(\dfrac17-\dfrac23+1-\dfrac43+4=\dfrac{22}{7}\). The last term gives \(\int_0^1\dfrac{4}{1+x^2}dx=4\cdot\dfrac{\pi}{4}=\pi\), so the integral is \(\dfrac{22}{7}-\pi\).
The integrand \(\dfrac{x^4(1-x)^4}{1+x^2}\) is positive for \(0<x<1\), so the integral is positive: \(\dfrac{22}{7}-\pi>0\).
Therefore \(\dfrac{22}{7}>\pi\): the fraction is an overestimate. Proof complete.

options: \(\begin{aligned}&u=\dfrac{1}{x},\ dx=-\dfrac{du}{u^{2}};\ x=\dfrac{1}{2}\to u=2,\ x=1\to u=1\\ &\int\dfrac{\ln\dfrac{1}{u}}{1+\dfrac{1}{u^{2}}}\left(-\dfrac{du}{u^{2}}\right)=\int_{2}^{1}\dfrac{-\ln u\cdot u^{2}}{u^{2}+1}\cdot\dfrac{-1}{u^{2}}du=\int_{2}^{1}\dfrac{\ln u}{1+u^{2}}du\end{aligned}\)

\(\begin{aligned}&u=\dfrac{1}{x},\ dx=\dfrac{du}{u^{2}};\ x=\dfrac{1}{2}\to u=2,\ x=1\to u=1\\ &\int\dfrac{\ln\dfrac{1}{u}}{1+\dfrac{1}{u^{2}}}\cdot\dfrac{du}{u^{2}}=\int_{2}^{1}\dfrac{\ln u}{1+u^{2}}du\end{aligned}\)

\(\begin{aligned}&u=\dfrac{1}{x},\ dx=-\dfrac{du}{u^{2}};\ x=\dfrac{1}{2}\to u=\dfrac{1}{2},\ x=1\to u=1\\ &\int\dfrac{\ln\dfrac{1}{u}}{1+\dfrac{1}{u^{2}}}\left(-\dfrac{du}{u^{2}}\right)=\int_{\frac12}^{1}\dfrac{\ln u}{1+u^{2}}du\end{aligned}\)
questions.hint: Everything in \(x\) must become \(u\): \(x=\dfrac{1}{u}\), \(dx=-\dfrac{1}{u^{2}}du\), and the limits change too. Use \(\ln\dfrac{1}{u}=-\ln u\). The two minus signs will cancel.

steps.explain: \(u=\dfrac{1}{x}\Rightarrow x=\dfrac{1}{u}\) and \(\dfrac{du}{dx}=-\dfrac{1}{x^{2}}=-u^{2}\), so \(dx=-\dfrac{1}{u^{2}}du\).
New limits: \(x=\dfrac{1}{2}\Rightarrow u=2\); \(x=1\Rightarrow u=1\).
Rewrite the integrand: \(\ln x=\ln\dfrac{1}{u}=-\ln u\) and \(1+x^{2}=1+\dfrac{1}{u^{2}}=\dfrac{u^{2}+1}{u^{2}}\).
Multiply by \(dx=-\dfrac{du}{u^{2}}\): the \(u^{2}\) cancels and \((-)(-)=+\).
Assemble with the new limits.
Why not the others: B loses the \(-\) from \(dx\) (sign error); C writes \(dx=+\dfrac{du}{u^{2}}\); D forgets to change the limits.

Reversing the limits flips the sign: \(\displaystyle\int_{2}^{1}=-\int_{1}^{2}\).
The two pieces are opposites and cancel.

questions.stem: Let \(I_{n}=\displaystyle\int_{0}^{a}x^{n}\sqrt{a^{2}-x^{2}}\,dx,\ a\in\mathbb{R}^{+}\) and \(n=0,1,2,\dots\) Prove that, for \(n=2,3,4,\dots\), \(I_{n}=\dfrac{a^{2}(n-1)}{n+2}I_{n-2}\). Which working is correct?
options: By parts: \(u=x^{n-1},\ v'=x\sqrt{a^{2}-x^{2}}\), so \(u'=(n-1)x^{n-2}\) and \(v=-\dfrac{1}{3}\left(a^{2}-x^{2}\right)^{\frac{3}{2}}\). \(I_{n}=\left[-\dfrac{x^{n-1}}{3}\left(a^{2}-x^{2}\right)^{\frac{3}{2}}\right]_{0}^{a}+\dfrac{n-1}{3}\int_{0}^{a}x^{n-2}\left(a^{2}-x^{2}\right)\sqrt{a^{2}-x^{2}}\,dx\). The bracket is 0 at both limits. So \(I_{n}=\dfrac{n-1}{3}\left[a^{2}I_{n-2}-I_{n}\right]\Rightarrow(n+2)I_{n}=a^{2}(n-1)I_{n-2}\).

By parts with \(u=\sqrt{a^{2}-x^{2}},\ v'=x^{n}\): \(I_{n}=\left[\dfrac{x^{n+1}}{n+1}\sqrt{a^{2}-x^{2}}\right]_{0}^{a}+\dfrac{1}{n+1}\int_{0}^{a}\dfrac{x^{n+2}}{\sqrt{a^{2}-x^{2}}}dx\), which is not in terms of \(I_{n-2}\), so the method fails.

By parts: \(u=x^{n-1},\ v=-\dfrac{1}{3}\left(a^{2}-x^{2}\right)^{\frac{3}{2}}\). Ignoring the boundary term (it is not zero): \(I_{n}=\dfrac{n-1}{3}\left[a^{2}I_{n-2}-I_{n}\right]\) and the result follows.
questions.hint: Split \(x^{n}\sqrt{a^{2}-x^{2}}=x^{n-1}\cdot x\sqrt{a^{2}-x^{2}}\). Integrate \(x\sqrt{a^{2}-x^{2}}\) (reverse chain rule) and differentiate \(x^{n-1}\). Show the boundary term is zero, then rewrite \(a^{2}-x^{2}\) using \(a^{2}-x^{2}\) times \(\sqrt{\cdot}\).

steps.explain: Choose \(u=x^{n-1}\) (differentiate down to \(x^{n-2}\)) and \(v'=x\sqrt{a^{2}-x^{2}}\) (integrate by reverse chain rule: \(\dfrac{d}{dx}\left(a^{2}-x^{2}\right)^{\frac{3}{2}}=-3x\sqrt{a^{2}-x^{2}}\)).
By parts: \(I_{n}=\left[uv\right]_{0}^{a}-\int u'v\,dx\).
Boundary term: at \(x=a\), \(\left(a^{2}-a^{2}\right)^{\frac{3}{2}}=0\); at \(x=0\), \(x^{n-1}=0\) (since \(n\ge2\)). Both are 0, so the bracket is 0.
Write \(\left(a^{2}-x^{2}\right)^{\frac{3}{2}}=\left(a^{2}-x^{2}\right)\sqrt{a^{2}-x^{2}}\) and split.
Solve for \(I_{n}\): multiply by 3 and bring the \(I_{n}\) terms together: \(3I_{n}+(n-1)I_{n}=(n-1)a^{2}I_{n-2}\).
Why not the others: B picks the wrong \(u\) and \(v'\); C gets \(n-2\) (a slip: \(3+(n-1)=n+2\)); D claims the boundary term is not zero (it is).
So the correct choice is option A.

keyPoints.note: By parts with u = x to the n minus 1; boundary term vanishes; then rewrite with a squared minus x squared.

questions.stem: Let \(I_{n}=\displaystyle\int_{0}^{a}x^{n}\sqrt{a^{2}-x^{2}}\,dx,\ a\in\mathbb{R}^{+}\) and \(n=0,1,2,\dots\) Prove that, for \(n=0,1,2,\dots\), \(I_{2n}=\pi\left(\dfrac{a}{2}\right)^{2n+2}\dfrac{(2n)!}{n!\,(n+1)!}\). Which working is correct?
options: Apply the recurrence down to \(I_{0}\) as before but use \(I_{0}=\dfrac{1}{2}\pi a^{2}\) (a semicircle). The result is \(I_{2n}=2\pi\left(\dfrac{a}{2}\right)^{2n+2}\dfrac{(2n)!}{n!(n+1)!}\), which is twice the required value.
Apply \(I_{n}=\dfrac{a^{2}(n-1)}{n+2}I_{n-2}\) with \(n\) instead of \(2n\): \(I_{2n}=\dfrac{a^{2}(n-1)}{n+2}I_{2n-2}\), and continue until \(I_{0}\).
Work out \(I_{0},I_{2},I_{4}\) by integration by parts and notice the pattern; this proves the formula for all \(n\).
questions.hint: Use the reduction formula from (i) repeatedly: \(I_{2n}\to I_{2n-2}\to\cdots\to I_{0}\). Evaluate \(I_{0}=\int_{0}^{a}\sqrt{a^{2}-x^{2}}dx\) as a geometric area (a quarter circle). Then turn the products of odd and even numbers into factorials.

steps.explain: Apply the reduction formula with \(n\to2n\): \(I_{2n}=\dfrac{a^{2}(2n-1)}{2n+2}I_{2n-2}\), then \(I_{2n-2}=\dfrac{a^{2}(2n-3)}{2n}I_{2n-4}\), and so on down to \(I_{2}=\dfrac{a^{2}(1)}{4}I_{0}\).
There are \(n\) factors, so the \(a^{2}\)s combine to \(a^{2n}\). Numerator: odd numbers \(1\cdot3\cdots(2n-1)\); denominator: even numbers \(4\cdot6\cdots(2n+2)\).
\(I_{0}=\int_{0}^{a}\sqrt{a^{2}-x^{2}}\,dx\) is the area of a QUARTER circle of radius \(a\).
Convert to factorials: \(1\cdot3\cdots(2n-1)=\dfrac{(2n)!}{2\cdot4\cdots2n}=\dfrac{(2n)!}{2^{n}n!}\) and \(4\cdot6\cdots(2n+2)=2^{n}\cdot2\cdot3\cdots(n+1)=2^{n}(n+1)!\).
Combine the powers: \(2^{n}\cdot2^{n}\cdot4=2^{2n+2}\) and \(a^{2n}\cdot a^{2}=a^{2n+2}\).
Why not the others: B uses a semicircle for \(I_{0}\); C does not replace \(n\) by \(2n\) consistently; D checks a few cases (not a proof).
So the correct choice is option A.

keyPoints.note: Apply the reduction formula repeatedly; I zero is a quarter circle; use factorials.

questions.stem: Let \(I_{n}=\displaystyle\int_{0}^{a}x^{n}\sqrt{a^{2}-x^{2}}\,dx,\ a\in\mathbb{R}^{+}\) and \(n=0,1,2,\dots\) \(C_{n}=\dfrac{1}{n+1}\dbinom{2n}{n}\) denotes the Catalan numbers. Prove that \(C_{n}=\dfrac{1}{\pi}\displaystyle\int_{0}^{2}x^{2n}\sqrt{4-x^{2}}\,dx\). Which working is correct?
options: From (ii) with \(a=2\): \(I_{2n}=\pi\dfrac{(2n)!}{n!(n+1)!}\). Since \(\dbinom{2n}{n}=\dfrac{(2n)!}{n!\,n!}\), \(C_{n}=\dfrac{1}{\pi}I_{2n}\) follows immediately with no further working.
\(C_{n}=\dfrac{1}{n+1}\dbinom{2n}{n}=\dfrac{(2n)!}{(n+1)!\,(n+1)!}\). With \(a=2\) in (ii), \(\dfrac{1}{\pi}I_{2n}=\dfrac{(2n)!}{n!(n+1)!}\), so these are equal.
questions.hint: Write \(C_{n}\) with factorials: \(\dbinom{2n}{n}=\dfrac{(2n)!}{n!\,n!}\), then combine \(\dfrac{1}{n+1}\) with one \(n!\) to get \((n+1)!\). Compare with part (ii) where \(a=2\) (since \(\sqrt{4-x^{2}}=\sqrt{2^{2}-x^{2}}\)).

steps.explain: Write the Catalan number in factorial form: \(\dbinom{2n}{n}=\dfrac{(2n)!}{n!\,(2n-n)!}=\dfrac{(2n)!}{n!\,n!}\).
Combine \(\dfrac{1}{n+1}\) with \(\dfrac{1}{n!}\): \((n+1)\cdot n!=(n+1)!\).
Divide by \(\pi\) and compare.
Why not the others: B skips the factorial manipulation; C uses \(a=4\) (the integral has \(\sqrt{4-x^{2}}\), so \(a=2\)); D simplifies \(C_{n}\) incorrectly.
So the correct choice is option A.

keyPoints.note: Express the Catalan number with factorials, then use part (ii) with a = 2.

steps.explain: \(I_{0}=\displaystyle\int_{0}^{\frac{\pi}{2}}\dfrac{dx}{2+\sin x}=\dfrac{1}{2}\int_{0}^{\frac{\pi}{2}}\dfrac{dx}{1+\dfrac{1}{2}\sin x}\). Use part (iii) with \(k=\dfrac{1}{2}\): \(\sqrt{1-k^{2}}=\dfrac{\sqrt3}{2}\) and \(\sqrt{\dfrac{1-k}{1+k}}=\dfrac{1}{\sqrt3}\).

Recurrence with \(n=1\): \(I_{2}+2I_{1}=\int_{0}^{\frac{\pi}{2}}\sin x\,dx=\left[-\cos x\right]_{0}^{\frac{\pi}{2}}=1\).
Substitute \(I_{1}\): \(1-2\left(\dfrac{\pi}{2}-\dfrac{2\sqrt3\pi}{9}\right)=1-\pi+\dfrac{4\sqrt3\pi}{9}\).

Check numerically: \(\dfrac{4\sqrt3}{9}\approx0.7698\), so \(I_{2}\approx(-0.2302)(3.1416)+1\approx0.277\), and the integrand \(\dfrac{\sin^{2}x}{2+\sin x}\) is between 0 and \(\dfrac{1}{3}\) with average about \(0.18\), over a length \(1.57\) ✓ (\(\approx0.28\)). Why not the others: B has the wrong sign on 1; C has \(\dfrac{2\sqrt3}{9}\) (forgot to double \(I_{0}\)); D has \(-1\) instead of \(+1\).
So the correct choice is option A.

options: Replace \(n\) by \(n+2\): \((n+3)I_{n+2}=\dfrac\pi4-\displaystyle\int_{0}^{1}\dfrac{x^{n+3}}{1+x^{2}}dx\). Add to the original: RHS \(=\dfrac\pi2-\displaystyle\int_{0}^{1}\dfrac{x^{n+1}+x^{n+3}}{1+x^{2}}dx=\dfrac\pi2-\displaystyle\int_{0}^{1}x^{n+1}dx=\dfrac\pi2-\dfrac{1}{n+2}\).
Replace \(n\) by \(n+2\) and add: RHS \(=\dfrac\pi2-\displaystyle\int_{0}^{1}x^{n+1}dx\), and \(\displaystyle\int_{0}^{1}x^{n+1}dx=\dfrac{1}{n+1}\), so the result is \(\dfrac\pi2-\dfrac{1}{n+1}\).
Replace \(n\) by \(n+2\) and SUBTRACT the two equations: RHS \(=0-\displaystyle\int_{0}^{1}x^{n+1}dx\), giving \(-\dfrac{1}{n+2}\).
questions.hint: Write the formula a second time with \(n\) replaced by \(n+2\), then ADD the two equations. The two integrals combine because \(x^{n+1}+x^{n+3}=x^{n+1}\left(1+x^{2}\right)\), which cancels the denominator \(1+x^{2}\).

steps.explain: Original formula (A).
Replace \(n\) by \(n+2\) everywhere: \(n+1\to n+3\) and \(n+1\) in the power \(\to n+3\).
Add the two equations. The \(\dfrac\pi4\) terms give \(\dfrac\pi2\) and the two integrals combine over the common denominator.
Factor the numerator: \(x^{n+1}+x^{n+3}=x^{n+1}\left(1+x^{2}\right)\), so the fraction simplifies to \(x^{n+1}\).
Integrate: \(\int_{0}^{1}x^{n+1}dx=\left[\dfrac{x^{n+2}}{n+2}\right]_{0}^{1}=\dfrac{1}{n+2}\).

Why not the others: B integrates \(x^{n+1}\) to \(\dfrac{1}{n+1}\) (the power rule gives \(\dfrac{x^{n+2}}{n+2}\)); C subtracts instead of adding; D keeps \(\dfrac\pi4\) (it is \(\dfrac\pi4+\dfrac\pi4=\dfrac\pi2\)).
So the correct choice is option A.

keyPoints.note: Add the formula for \(n\) and for \(n+2\); \(x^{n+1}(1+x^2)\) cancels.

Substitute into (i): \(I_{n}=\dfrac{1}{2^{n}}+2n\int_{0}^{1}\dfrac{x^{2}}{(1+x^{2})^{n+1}}dx\).
Expand and collect the \(I_{n+1}\) term on one side: \(I_{n}=\dfrac1{2^{n}}+2nI_{n}-2nI_{n+1}\).

questions.stem: If \(I_{n}=\displaystyle\int_{1}^{e}(1-\ln x)^{n}\,dx\) for \(n=0,1,2,\dots\) show that \(I_{n}=-1+nI_{n-1}\). Which working is correct?
options: By parts with \(u=(1-\ln x)^{n}\), \(v'=1\): \(u'=n(1-\ln x)^{n-1}\cdot\left(-\dfrac{1}{x}\right)\), \(v=x\). Then \(I_{n}=\left[x(1-\ln x)^{n}\right]_{1}^{e}+n\displaystyle\int_{1}^{e}(1-\ln x)^{n-1}dx=(0-1)+nI_{n-1}=-1+nI_{n-1}\).

By parts with \(u=(1-\ln x)^{n}\), \(v'=1\): \(u'=n(1-\ln x)^{n-1}\left(-\dfrac{1}{x}\right)\), \(v=x\). Then \(I_{n}=\left[x(1-\ln x)^{n}\right]_{1}^{e}-n\displaystyle\int_{1}^{e}(1-\ln x)^{n-1}dx=-1-nI_{n-1}\).
By parts with \(u=(1-\ln x)^{n}\), \(v'=1\): the boundary term is \(\left[x(1-\ln x)^{n}\right]_{1}^{e}=e\cdot0-0=0\), so \(I_{n}=nI_{n-1}\).
By parts with \(u=1\), \(v'=(1-\ln x)^{n}\): \(v=\dfrac{(1-\ln x)^{n+1}}{n+1}\), which gives \(I_{n}=-1+nI_{n-1}\) directly.
questions.hint: Integrate by parts with \(u=(1-\ln x)^{n}\) and \(v'=1\) (so \(v=x\)). The chain rule gives the factor \(-\dfrac{1}{x}\), which cancels the \(x\) in \(vu'\). Evaluate the boundary term carefully at BOTH limits \(1\) and \(e\).

steps.explain: The \(x\) cancels with \(\dfrac{1}{x}\), and \(-\)(negative) \(=+\): the integral becomes \(+n\int_{1}^{e}(1-\ln x)^{n-1}dx=+nI_{n-1}\).
Boundary term: at \(x=e\): \(e(1-1)^{n}=0\) (for \(n\ge1\)). At \(x=1\): \(1\cdot(1-0)^{n}=1\). So the bracket is \(0-1=-1\).
Combine.

Why not the others: B has the wrong sign on the integral (a minus times the negative \(u'\) is a PLUS); C evaluates the lower limit as 0 instead of 1; D chooses \(u=1\), \(v'=(1-\ln x)^{n}\), which is not possible (that integral is not elementary).
So the correct choice is option A.

keyPoints.note: \(u=(1-\ln x)^n\), \(v=x\); boundary term \(=0-1\).

questions.stem: Let \(I_{n}=\displaystyle\int_{0}^{1}\left(1-t^{2}\right)^{\frac{n-1}{2}}dt\), where \(n\) is a non-negative integer. Using integration by parts, or otherwise, show that \(nI_{n}=(n-1)I_{n-2}\) if \(n\ge2\). Which working is correct?
options: By parts with \(u=\left(1-t^{2}\right)^{\frac{n-1}{2}}\), \(v'=1\): \(u'=\dfrac{n-1}{2}\left(1-t^{2}\right)^{\frac{n-3}{2}}(-2t)\), \(v=t\). \(I_{n}=\left[t\left(1-t^{2}\right)^{\frac{n-1}{2}}\right]_{0}^{1}+(n-1)\displaystyle\int_{0}^{1}t^{2}\left(1-t^{2}\right)^{\frac{n-3}{2}}dt\). The bracket is 0 (\(n\ge2\)). Write \(t^{2}=1-\left(1-t^{2}\right)\): the integral is \(I_{n-2}-I_{n}\). So \(I_{n}=(n-1)\left(I_{n-2}-I_{n}\right)\), i.e. \(nI_{n}=(n-1)I_{n-2}\).

By parts as above, but with the integral \(-(n-1)\displaystyle\int t^{2}\left(1-t^{2}\right)^{\frac{n-3}{2}}dt\). Then \(I_{n}=-(n-1)\left(I_{n-2}-I_{n}\right)\), which gives \((n-2)I_{n}=-(n-1)I_{n-2}\).
By parts as above, with the boundary term \(\left[t\left(1-t^{2}\right)^{\frac{n-1}{2}}\right]_{0}^{1}=1\). Then \(I_{n}=1+(n-1)\left(I_{n-2}-I_{n}\right)\).
Replace \(t^{2}\) by \(1+\left(1-t^{2}\right)\): the integral becomes \(I_{n-2}+I_{n}\), so \(I_{n}=(n-1)\left(I_{n-2}+I_{n}\right)\).
questions.hint: Parts with \(u=\left(1-t^{2}\right)^{\frac{n-1}{2}}\), \(v'=1\), \(v=t\). The chain rule gives a factor \(-2t\), creating \(t^{2}\). Then write \(t^{2}=1-\left(1-t^{2}\right)\) to split the new integral into \(I_{n-2}\) and \(I_{n}\). Check the boundary term at \(t=1\) and \(t=0\).

steps.explain: Boundary term: at \(t=1\): \(1\cdot0^{\frac{n-1}{2}}=0\) (the exponent \(\dfrac{n-1}{2}\ge\dfrac{1}{2}>0\) for \(n\ge2\)); at \(t=0\): 0. Minus a negative gives plus.
Write \(t^{2}=1-\left(1-t^{2}\right)\) and distribute: \(\left(1-t^{2}\right)^{\frac{n-3}{2}}-\left(1-t^{2}\right)^{\frac{n-3}{2}+1}\), and \(\dfrac{n-3}{2}+1=\dfrac{n-1}{2}\).
Substitute and collect \(I_{n}\) terms on the left: \(I_{n}+(n-1)I_{n}=(n-1)I_{n-2}\).
Why not the others: B has the wrong sign (the double negative gives PLUS); C has the wrong boundary value (it is 0, not 1); D uses \(t^{2}=1+\left(1-t^{2}\right)\) (it is \(1-\left(1-t^{2}\right)\)).
So the correct choice is option A.

questions.stem: Let \(I_{n}=\displaystyle\int_{0}^{1}\left(1-t^{2}\right)^{\frac{n-1}{2}}dt\) with \(nI_{n}=(n-1)I_{n-2}\) for \(n\ge2\), and let \(J_{n}=nI_{n}I_{n-1}\), \(n\ge1\). Show that \(J_{n}=\dfrac\pi2\), \(\forall n\ge1\). Which argument is correct?
options: For \(n\ge2\): \(J_{n}=nI_{n}I_{n-1}=(n-1)I_{n-2}I_{n-1}=(n-1)I_{n-1}I_{n-2}=J_{n-1}\). So all \(J_{n}\) are equal to \(J_{1}\). \(J_{1}=1\cdot I_{1}I_{0}\), where \(I_{1}=\displaystyle\int_{0}^{1}1\,dt=1\) and \(I_{0}=\displaystyle\int_{0}^{1}\dfrac{dt}{\sqrt{1-t^{2}}}=\sin^{-1}1=\dfrac\pi2\). So \(J_{n}=\dfrac\pi2\) for all \(n\ge1\).

For \(n\ge2\): \(J_{n}=nI_{n}I_{n-1}=(n-1)I_{n-2}I_{n-1}=J_{n-1}\). \(J_{1}=I_{1}I_{0}\) where \(I_{1}=\displaystyle\int_{0}^{1}1\,dt=1\) and \(I_{0}=\sin^{-1}1=\dfrac\pi2\), but then \(J_{n}=\pi\) by doubling.
For \(n\ge2\): \(J_{n}=nI_{n}I_{n-1}=(n-1)I_{n}I_{n-1}\), so \(J_{n}=\dfrac{n-1}{n}J_{n}\), which means \(J_{n}\) is not constant.
questions.hint: Show \(J_{n}=J_{n-1}\) using \(nI_{n}=(n-1)I_{n-2}\) (substitute for \(nI_{n}\)). Then every \(J_{n}\) equals \(J_{1}\); compute \(J_{1}=I_{1}I_{0}\) from the definitions (\(I_{1}=\int1\,dt\); \(I_{0}\) is a \(\sin^{-1}\) integral).

steps.explain: Replace \(nI_{n}\) by \((n-1)I_{n-2}\) inside \(J_{n}\).
Rearrange the factors: \((n-1)I_{n-2}\,I_{n-1}=\left((n-1)\,I_{n-1}\,I_{n-2}\right)\), which is exactly \(J_{n-1}=(n-1)I_{n-1}I_{n-2}\).
Therefore \(J_{1}=1\times\dfrac\pi2\), and all \(J_{n}\) equal it.
Why not the others: B doubles for no reason; C misapplies the recurrence (\(nI_{n}\to(n-1)I_{n}\) is wrong, it is \((n-1)I_{n-2}\)); D takes \(I_{0}=1\) (it is \(\dfrac\pi2\)).
So the correct choice is option A.

keyPoints.note: \(J_n=J_{n-1}\) using the recurrence; \(J_1=I_1I_0=\dfrac\pi2\).

steps.explain: Let \(I\) be the integral. Replace \(x\) by \(\pi-x\) using part (i); \(\sin(\pi-x)=\sin x\) and \(\cos(\pi-x)=-\cos x\) so \(\cos^{2}(\pi-x)=\cos^{2}x\).
Add the two expressions for \(I\): \(x+(\pi-x)=\pi\), so the \(x\) disappears.
Substitute \(u=\cos x\), \(du=-\sin x\,dx\). Limits: \(x=0\Rightarrow u=1\); \(x=\pi\Rightarrow u=-1\).
\(\displaystyle\int\dfrac{du}{1+u^{2}}=\tan^{-1}u\), so evaluate between \(-1\) and \(1\).
So \(2I=\pi\times\dfrac{\pi}{2}=\dfrac{\pi^{2}}{2}\), giving \(I=\dfrac{\pi^{2}}{4}\).
Why not the others: B forgets to divide by 2 (that is \(2I\)); C and D lose a factor of \(\pi\) or use \(\int=\dfrac{\pi}{4}\) only once.
So the correct choice is option A.

questions.hint: Recognise \(\dfrac{1-\tan x}{1+\tan x}=\dfrac{\tan\dfrac{\pi}{4}-\tan x}{1+\tan\dfrac{\pi}{4}\tan x}=\tan\left(\dfrac{\pi}{4}-x\right)\) (compound-angle formula), or convert to sin and cos.

steps.explain: Since \(\tan\dfrac{\pi}{4}=1\), use \(\tan(A-B)=\dfrac{\tan A-\tan B}{1+\tan A\tan B}\) with \(A=\dfrac{\pi}{4}\).
Integrate: \(\int\tan u\,du=-\ln|\cos u|\). Here \(u=\dfrac{\pi}{4}-x\) with \(\dfrac{du}{dx}=-1\), so \(\int\tan\left(\dfrac{\pi}{4}-x\right)dx=+\ln\left|\cos\left(\dfrac{\pi}{4}-x\right)\right|\).
At \(x=\dfrac{\pi}{4}\): \(\ln\cos0=\ln1=0\). At \(x=0\): \(\ln\cos\dfrac{\pi}{4}=\ln\dfrac{1}{\sqrt2}=-\dfrac{1}{2}\ln2\).

Alternative: \(\dfrac{1-\tan x}{1+\tan x}=\dfrac{\cos x-\sin x}{\cos x+\sin x}\), and the top is the derivative of the bottom, so the integral is \(\left[\ln(\cos x+\sin x)\right]_{0}^{\frac{\pi}{4}}=\ln\sqrt2-\ln1=\dfrac{1}{2}\ln2\) ✓.
Why not the others: B forgets \(\ln\sqrt2=\dfrac{1}{2}\ln2\); C and D confuse the integral with \(\int1\,dx\) or lose the sign from \(du=-dx\).
So the correct choice is option A.

questions.stem: Consider the curve \(y=f(x)\), where \(f(x)=\dfrac{1}{1+\cos x+\sin x}\). The area of the region \(R_{1}\), bounded by the \(x\)-axis, the \(y\)-axis, the line \(x=\dfrac{\pi}{2}\) and the curve \(y=f(x)\), is \(\ln2\) units\(^{2}\). The region \(R_{2}\) is bounded by the \(x\)-axis, the line \(x=\dfrac{\pi}{2}\) and the curve \(y=xf(x)\). Prove that the ratio of the area of \(R_{1}\) to the area of \(R_{2}\) is \(4:\pi\).
questions.hint: \(A_{2}=\displaystyle\int_{0}^{\frac{\pi}{2}}xf(x)\,dx\) cannot be done directly. Use the KING PROPERTY \(\displaystyle\int_{0}^{a}h(x)dx=\int_{0}^{a}h(a-x)dx\) with \(a=\dfrac{\pi}{2}\): \(f\) is symmetric because \(f\!\left(\dfrac\pi2-x\right)=\dfrac{1}{1+\sin x+\cos x}=f(x)\). Then ADD the two forms of \(A_{2}\).

steps.explain: Area of \(R_{1}\) is given: \(A_{1}=\displaystyle\int_{0}^{\frac{\pi}{2}}f(x)dx=\ln2\). Area of \(R_{2}\): \(A_{2}=\displaystyle\int_{0}^{\frac{\pi}{2}}xf(x)dx\).
Symmetry of \(f\): \(f\!\left(\dfrac\pi2-x\right)=\dfrac{1}{1+\cos\left(\dfrac\pi2-x\right)+\sin\left(\dfrac\pi2-x\right)}=\dfrac{1}{1+\sin x+\cos x}=f(x)\).
King property with \(a=\dfrac\pi2\): replace \(x\) by \(\dfrac\pi2-x\) in the integrand of \(A_{2}\).
Add the two expressions for \(A_{2}\): \(x+\left(\dfrac\pi2-x\right)=\dfrac\pi2\), so the \(x\) cancels.
Why not the others: B stops at \(2A_{2}=\dfrac\pi2A_{1}\) without dividing by 2 (giving \(2:\pi\)); C only proves an inequality; D wrongly integrates \(x\) alone and ignores \(f\).
So the correct choice is option A.

questions.stem: The value of \(\dfrac{d}{dx}\left(\displaystyle\int_{x}^{2x}\dfrac{1}{1+t^{2}}\,dt\right)\) is which of the following?
questions.hint: Let \(F(t)\) be an antiderivative of \(\dfrac{1}{1+t^{2}}\). Then the integral equals \(F(2x)-F(x)\). Differentiate with the CHAIN RULE: \(\dfrac{d}{dx}F(2x)=2F'(2x)\).

steps.explain: Let \(F'(t)=\dfrac{1}{1+t^{2}}\) (e.g. \(F(t)=\tan^{-1}t\)). The definite integral is \(F(\text{top})-F(\text{bottom})\).
Differentiate \(\tan^{-1}(2x)\) using the chain rule: \(\dfrac{d}{dx}\tan^{-1}(u)=\dfrac{u'}{1+u^{2}}\) with \(u=2x\), \(u'=2\).
Differentiate \(-\tan^{-1}x\).
Combine.
Why not the others: C forgets the chain-rule factor 2; D has a plus sign (the LOWER limit gives a minus); A ignores the upper limit \(2x\).
So the correct choice is option B.

questions.stem: Prove that \(\displaystyle\int_{a}^{b}f(x)\,dx=\dfrac{1}{2}\int_{a}^{b}\left\{f(x)+f(a+b-x)\right\}dx\). Which proof is correct?
options: Let \(u=a+b-x\), so \(du=-dx\); when \(x=a\), \(u=b\), and when \(x=b\), \(u=a\). Then \(\displaystyle\int_{a}^{b}f(x)dx=-\int_{b}^{a}f(a+b-u)du=\int_{a}^{b}f(a+b-u)du\). Adding this to the original gives \(2\displaystyle\int_{a}^{b}f(x)dx=\int_{a}^{b}\{f(x)+f(a+b-x)\}dx\); divide by 2.
Let \(u=a+b-x\), so \(du=dx\); the limits stay \(a\) and \(b\). Then \(\displaystyle\int_{a}^{b}f(x)dx=\int_{a}^{b}f(a+b-u)du\). Adding gives the result.
Let \(u=a-b-x\), so \(du=-dx\), \(x=a\Rightarrow u=-b\) and \(x=b\Rightarrow u=-a\). The result follows by adding.
Since \(f(a+b-x)=f(x)\) for every function \(f\), the two integrals are equal and the result follows.
questions.hint: Use the substitution \(u=a+b-x\). It maps the interval \([a,b]\) onto itself in REVERSE (a becomes b, b becomes a). Then add the new integral to the original.

steps.explain: Let \(u=a+b-x\). Then \(du=-dx\) and the limits become: \(x=a\Rightarrow u=b\); \(x=b\Rightarrow u=a\).
The minus sign lets us swap the limits back (\(-\int_{b}^{a}=\int_{a}^{b}\)). The name of the variable does not matter, so rename \(u\) as \(x\).
Add this to \(I=\int_{a}^{b}f(x)\,dx\).
Divide by 2.
Why not the others: B has \(du=dx\) and unchanged limits (wrong); C uses \(a-b-x\) (that is not a reflection of \([a,b]\)); D is false in general (e.g. \(f(x)=x\)).
So the correct choice is option A.

keyPoints.note: Substitute \(u=a+b-x\): limits swap.

questions.stem: Which of the following is false? (A) \(\displaystyle\int_{-3}^{3}x^{3}e^{-x^{2}}dx=0\) (B) \(\displaystyle\int_{-4}^{4}\dfrac{x^{2}}{x^{2}+4}dx=2\displaystyle\int_{0}^{4}\dfrac{x^{2}}{x^{2}+4}dx\) (C) \(\displaystyle\int_{0}^{\pi}\sin^{4}\theta\,d\theta>\displaystyle\int_{0}^{\pi}\sin4\theta\,d\theta\) (D) \(\displaystyle\int_{0}^{1}x^{4}dx<\displaystyle\int_{0}^{1}x^{5}dx\)
questions.hint: Check each one. ODD function over a symmetric interval \(\Rightarrow\) integral \(=0\). EVEN function \(\Rightarrow\) \(\int_{-a}^{a}=2\int_{0}^{a}\). For inequalities, compute both sides or compare the integrands.

steps.explain: (A) \(f(x)=x^{3}e^{-x^{2}}\): \(f(-x)=(-x)^{3}e^{-x^{2}}=-f(x)\), an ODD function, over \([-3,3]\) (symmetric): the integral is 0. TRUE.

(C) \(\int_{0}^{\pi}\sin^{4}\theta\,d\theta=\dfrac{3\pi}{8}>0\) (the integrand \(\ge0\)), but \(\int_{0}^{\pi}\sin4\theta\,d\theta=\left[-\dfrac{\cos4\theta}{4}\right]_{0}^{\pi}=-\dfrac{1}{4}+\dfrac{1}{4}=0\). So \(\dfrac{3\pi}{8}>0\) is TRUE.

(D) On \(0<x<1\): \(x^{4}>x^{5}\) (a number between 0 and 1 gets smaller with a higher power). So \(\int_{0}^{1}x^{4}dx=\dfrac{1}{5}>\dfrac{1}{6}=\int_{0}^{1}x^{5}dx\). The statement “\(<\)” is FALSE.
The false statement is (D).
Why not the others: A, B and C are all true (shown above).
So the correct choice is option D.
